steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the Defenses section of an encyclopedia article on ARP spoofing, covering static ARP entries, detection and prevention software, and how operating systems handle ARP messages.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Static ARP entries
- Detection and prevention software
- OS security

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Static ARP entries
  - simplest certification: static, read-only entries for critical services in host ARP cache
  - no ARP requests needed where such entries exist
  - some security, but more maintenance: mappings for all systems generated and distributed
  - doesn't scale: mapping per pair of machines -> n2-n entries for n machines; n-1 entries on each of n machines
- Detection and prevention software
  - certification or cross-checking of ARP responses; uncertified responses blocked
  - may integrate with DHCP server -> dynamic and static IPs certified
  - in individual hosts or in Ethernet switches / other network equipment
  - multiple IPs on one MAC may indicate spoofing (but legitimate uses exist)
  - passive: listen for ARP replies, email notification when entry changes
  - AntiARP: Windows, kernel level
  - ArpStar: Linux module, kernel 2.6 and Linksys routers, drops invalid packets violating mapping
  - virtualized environments (e.g. Kernel-based Virtual Machine): prevent MAC spoofing between guests on same host
  - some Ethernet adapters: MAC and VLAN anti-spoofing
  - OpenBSD: passively watches for hosts impersonating local host, notifies on attempt to overwrite permanent entry
- OS security
  - OSes react differently
  - Linux: ignores unsolicited replies, uses responses to requests from other machines to update cache
  - Solaris: updates only after timeout
  - Windows: configurable via registry entries

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
### Static ARP entries

The simplest kind of certification is to use static, read-only entries for critical services in the ARP cache of a host. Where there are such entries, the host does not need to send ARP requests. Static entries give some security against spoofing, but they make maintenance harder, because the address mappings for all of the systems in the network have to be generated and distributed. Doing this for all participants does not scale on a large network, since the mapping has to be set for every pair of machines. When n machines are present this means n2-n ARP entries to configure: every machine needs an ARP entry for every other machine on the network, so n-1 ARP entries on each of the n machines.

### Detection and prevention software

Software that detects ARP spoofing usually depends on some kind of certification or cross-checking of ARP responses, and uncertified ARP responses are then blocked. These techniques can be integrated with the DHCP server so that both dynamic and static IP addresses get certified. This can be implemented in individual hosts or it can be integrated into Ethernet switches or other network equipment. If there are multiple IP addresses associated with a single MAC address this may indicate an ARP spoof attack, but there are also legitimate uses of that configuration. A more passive approach is a device that listens for ARP replies on a network and sends a notification by email when an ARP entry changes.

- AntiARP: Windows-based prevention, kernel level
- ArpStar: Linux module, kernel 2.6 and Linksys routers, drops invalid packets violating mapping
- virtualized environments e.g. Kernel-based Virtual Machine: prevent MAC spoofing between guests on same host
- some Ethernet adapters: MAC and VLAN anti-spoofing
- OpenBSD: passively watches for hosts impersonating local host, notifies on attempt to overwrite permanent entry

### OS security

- OSes react differently to ARP messages
- Linux ignores unsolicited replies, uses responses to other machines' requests to update cache
- Solaris accepts updates only after timeout
- Windows: ARP cache behavior configured through registry entries

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
### Static ARP entries

The simplest kind of certification is to use static, read-only entries for critical services in the ARP cache of a host. Where there are such entries, the host does not need to send ARP requests. Static entries give some security against spoofing, but they make maintenance harder, because the address mappings for all of the systems in the network have to be generated and distributed. Doing this for all participants does not scale on a large network, since the mapping has to be set for every pair of machines. When n machines are present this means n2-n ARP entries to configure: every machine needs an ARP entry for every other machine on the network, so n-1 ARP entries on each of the n machines.

### Detection and prevention software

Software that detects ARP spoofing usually depends on some kind of certification or cross-checking of ARP responses, and uncertified ARP responses are then blocked. These techniques can be integrated with the DHCP server so that both dynamic and static IP addresses get certified. This can be implemented in individual hosts or it can be integrated into Ethernet switches or other network equipment. If there are multiple IP addresses associated with a single MAC address this may indicate an ARP spoof attack, but there are also legitimate uses of that configuration. A more passive approach is a device that listens for ARP replies on a network and sends a notification by email when an ARP entry changes.

AntiARP also gives Windows-based spoofing prevention at the kernel level. ArpStar is a Linux module for kernel 2.6 and Linksys routers, and it drops invalid packets that violate the mapping.

Some virtualized environments, like the Kernel-based Virtual Machine, have security mechanisms that prevent MAC spoofing between guests running on the same host.

Some Ethernet adapters have MAC and VLAN anti-spoofing features.

OpenBSD passively watches for hosts that impersonate the local host and it gives a notification if anything tries to overwrite a permanent entry.

### OS security

Different operating systems react to ARP messages in different ways. Linux ignores unsolicited replies, but it does use responses to requests from other machines to update its cache. Solaris only accepts updates on entries after a timeout. In Microsoft Windows, how the ARP cache behaves can be configured with several registry entries.

steps.text:
### Static ARP entries

The simplest form of certification is the use of static, read-only entries for critical services in a host's ARP cache. Hosts don't need to transmit ARP requests where such entries exist.[1] While static entries provide some security against spoofing, they increase maintenance effort, since address mappings for all systems in the network must be generated and distributed. Securing ARP this way for all participants does not scale on a large network, because the mapping has to be set for each pair of machines, resulting in n2-n ARP entries to configure when n machines are present: on each machine there must be an ARP entry for every other machine on the network, so n-1 ARP entries on each of the n machines.

### Detection and prevention software

Software that detects ARP spoofing generally relies on some form of certification or cross-checking of ARP responses. Uncertified ARP responses are then blocked. These techniques may be integrated with the DHCP server so that both dynamic and static IP addresses are certified. This capability may be implemented in individual hosts or integrated into Ethernet switches or other network equipment. Multiple IP addresses associated with a single MAC address may indicate an ARP spoof attack, although such a configuration also has legitimate uses. In a more passive approach, a device listens for ARP replies on a network and sends a notification via email when an ARP entry changes.[2]

AntiARP[3] also provides Windows-based spoofing prevention at the kernel level. ArpStar is a Linux module for kernel 2.6 and Linksys routers that drops invalid packets violating the mapping.

Some virtualized environments, such as the Kernel-based Virtual Machine, provide security mechanisms that prevent MAC spoofing between guests running on the same host.[4]

Some Ethernet adapters provide MAC and VLAN anti-spoofing features.[5]

OpenBSD passively watches for hosts impersonating the local host and notifies in case of any attempt to overwrite a permanent entry.[6]

### OS security

Operating systems react differently to ARP messages. Linux ignores unsolicited replies but uses responses to requests from other machines to update its cache. Solaris accepts updates on entries only after a timeout. In Microsoft Windows, the behavior of the ARP cache can be configured through several registry entries.[7]
